description: We are Scirocco, a team of university students mapping the labyrinth of Mars. Combining our skills in software and planetary data analysis, we aim to build an intuitive exploration tool for the Red Planet.
summary:
Ariadne is a walking-scale Mars EVA map for Bright Angel in Jezero crater. It layers NASA data, plans a science walk, and shows at every moment whether the astronaut can still get back to the safe haven. It is for the people who plan a walk on Mars: the team at the mission console, and the astronaut, who sees the same clock on a phone worn as a wrist cuff. On Mars, every walk needs a way back.

We turned NASA HiRISE images and terrain of Jezero into slope, walking cost and minutes to home. The stops are places Perseverance studied, with its photos. As time passes, the map shrinks to the ground the astronaut can still reach and get back from. In our demo, a simulated storm alert sends both screens the way home. Every value carries its provenance. The walk values come from NASA lunar EVA requirements and a Mars suit (PLSS) design study, so it is a planning aid, not a safety tool.
details:
What it does

Ariadne is a map of one Mars walk that always knows the way home. For every 2 m of ground around Bright Angel in Jezero crater, where Perseverance found the Cheyava Falls rock, it computes the minutes back to the safe haven over the real HiRISE terrain, and it answers one question: if I go there now, can I still get back with my reserve? The mission console plans the walk; the astronaut carries it out with a phone worn as a wrist cuff, on the same clock. The site is 2.5 x 2 km.

There are two screens:

  • Mission console (laptop or projector). The site in 3D: the HiRISE terrain model, lit, with the HiRISE orthoimage draped over it, the return envelope, Perseverance's track, the planned route, the stops and the safe haven. Across the top: the mission clock, the margin to home and the next stop. A flat 2D map with every layer (hillshade, slope, go / caution / no-go ground, waypoints) is one click away. Side panels hold the layer list, a route table (each leg with distance, walking time and the time left), the conditions (weather, radiation, space weather) and the stop cards (science question, tasks and Perseverance photos with their credit lines).
  • Cuff (a phone worn on the wrist, paired by QR code). It shows the margin to home in minutes, the consumables left, the next stop and its card, and the storm-alert screen. Both screens share one clock.

The return envelope colours every part of the map: home with the reserve and time to spare, home with the reserve but little to spare, or no way home without using the reserve. It shrinks as the walk goes on. A toggle shows the same envelope on flat ground, so you can see what the terrain changes. A "seen, not touched" layer marks ground that Perseverance's cameras saw but the rover never drove to. Four targets on it have their own cards.

When the operator raises a storm alert, the console lights only the ground from which home can be reached before the storm and draws the way home ("the thread"), and the cuff switches to "Follow the thread home" with a countdown. In the demo the astronaut reaches the safe haven before the all-clear, and the walk ends there. (In a live session, if the astronaut is not home yet when the all-clear comes, the walk returns to the plan where it left it.)

Live site: https://ariadne-gilt-tau.vercel.app. Its services run on a cloud server that stays up through judging.

How it works

  1. Pipeline (Python, GDAL). It crops the USGS HiRISE orthomosaic (25 cm) and DTM (1 m) to our area. Slope is computed on the 1 m DTM with Horn's method; a 2 m cell takes the mean of its four 1 m slopes. Cells above 20° are no-go; 15–20° is caution. Walking speed is 2 km/h on flat ground and drops with slope. One shortest-path run from the safe haven gives the minutes home from every 2 m cell.
  2. Planner (Python, FastAPI). /route finds the least-cost path through the stops. /abort finds the path home from any point.
  3. Mission control (Go, Fiber). It runs the walk simulation and streams the state to both screens over WebSocket, twice a second. It also serves the conditions: Mars 2020 MEDA weather for sol 1215 (archive), a radiation value, and NASA DONKI CME arrival forecasts for Mars (live).
  4. Web (TypeScript, React, deck.gl). The console and the cuff. The envelope is computed in the browser: margin = budget − elapsed time − reserve − minutes home.

All positions are metres on a local plane. Every value on screen has a provenance label: Observed, Derived, Modeled, Assumed or Simulation.

On the real data (Modeled unless noted):

  • The planned walk from the safe haven through the five stops and back is 2.89 km: 119.7 min of walking plus 100 min at the stops, 219.7 min in all. That leaves 80.3 min before the 60 min reserve in a 360 min EVA.
  • 225 min into the EVA, with 75 min left before the reserve, home is still reachable from 52.0 % of the area over the real terrain. On flat ground it would be 94.4 %.
  • Along 4.51 km of Perseverance's own track, 1.6 % is steeper than our 20° limit (Derived). A rover is not a human, so this is a sanity check, not proof of safety.
  • Between Tuff Cliff and Bright Angel our planned leg is 581 m; the rover drove 582 m.

The demo video is a screen recording of the app running on the real data, with captions added. The map, the stops and the photos are real NASA data; the astronaut's walk is a simulation and the storm alert is simulated, raised by the operator. The app's DEMO replay (?demo=1) is SYNTHETIC data, marked "DEMO DATA" on screen, and is used only by the automated test. DONKI forecasts appear in the conditions panel in live mode only; they never raise the alert.

How it answers the challenge

  • A layered, integrated view from several NASA missions: MRO HiRISE image and terrain; Mars 2020 track, waypoints, Mastcam-Z and Navcam photos and MEDA weather; MSL RAD dose rate; NASA DONKI forecasts; all on one metre grid
  • Walking scale, not regional: One 2.5 x 2 km site, 1 m terrain, 2 m cost cells
  • A science goal and a place that fits it: The possible biosignature at Cheyava Falls, Bright Angel, Jezero
  • At least three data types: Optical, topographic, atmospheric, radiation, space weather
  • Safety: radiation and space weather: RAD dose rate (measured at Gale, Modeled for Jezero) and live DONKI CME arrivals for Mars shown beside the plan; a simulated storm alert lights the ground home is reachable from and draws the way home on both screens
  • Moving in a suit; a route that avoids obstacles: 20° no-go slope, slope-dependent walking speed, least-cost route, return envelope
  • A tablet or HUD: Mission console plus a phone worn as a wrist cuff
  • Plan and carry out: The console plans; the cuff carries it out on the same clock
  • Images through the rover's eyes: Perseverance's own photos at every stop and target
  • Rover support or buddy work: A pressurized rover is the safe haven; a crewmate at the console sees the same margin

Science. Bright Angel, on the northern edge of Neretva Vallis in Jezero crater, is where Perseverance found Cheyava Falls. This reddish mudstone has millimetre-size "leopard spots", and the rover took its Sapphire Canyon core from it on about sol 1215 (NASA, July 2024; Hurowitz et al. 2025, Nature). Did these spots form through chemistry that microbes could have used for energy, or without life? A rover found the clue. A geologist on foot could go back to test it.

Our walk follows Perseverance's own stops, in the rover's order: Mount Washburn, Tuff Cliff, Bright Angel, Cheyava Falls and Masonic Temple. Each stop card asks one science question from the NASA pages and papers, and lists the tasks a human would do there: the contact between two rock units, layer thicknesses with a scale bar, close-ups of the spots and veins. We also mapped ground that the rover's cameras saw but the rover never drove to. Four targets there are 22–46 min from the safe haven.

The walk model answers a planner's first question: does the walk fit, and how much is left over? The walk is 2.89 km: 119.7 min of walking plus 100 min at the stops, which leaves 80.3 min before the 60 min reserve (Modeled). It cannot say how a suited astronaut walks on Mars. No one has done it yet, so the speed, the slope limit and the EVA length come from lunar requirements and a Mars suit design study (Assumed). If a what-if suit leak or a dust storm cuts the time, the console suggests the smallest change that still gets the astronaut home with the reserve intact: shorter stops first, then skipping a stop. The crew decides.

Benefits

  • An EVA team could see, before the walk, what each stop costs in time and how much margin is left.
  • During the walk, the crew and the ground see the same picture: where the astronaut can still go and still get home.
  • If something goes wrong, the way home is already on the map.

Intended impact

Ariadne is a first step toward planning tools for human walks on the Moon and Mars. It shows how open NASA orbital data, rover data and EVA planning values can be combined into one decision: can we still get home from here?

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python, Go, TypeScript.
  • Data: GDAL, rasterio, pyproj, numpy, scikit-image, scipy, matplotlib.
  • Services: FastAPI and uvicorn (planner), Fiber (mission control), WebSocket.
  • Web: React, deck.gl, Vite, zustand, uqr (QR code).
  • Tests: pytest, Go test, Vitest, Playwright (end-to-end test of both screens through the storm alert).
  • Hosting: Vercel (web); Docker and Caddy on a Hetzner Cloud server (services).
  • Hardware: a laptop for the console, a phone for the cuff.
  • AI: Claude Code (see "How we used AI").

How it is creative

  • Not a radius, a shape. One shortest-path run from the safe haven gives the minutes home from every point. The return envelope bends around steep ground and shrinks every minute; on flat ground 94.4 % of the site looks reachable at T+225 min, over the real terrain only 52.0 %.
  • A thread home. In a storm the map lights only the ground from which home can be reached before the storm, and draws the way home on both screens.
  • Replanning as a suggestion. After a what-if suit leak or dust storm the console proposes the smallest change that keeps the reserve: shorter stops first, then skipping a stop. The crew decides.
  • Seen, not touched. We mark ground Perseverance's cameras saw but it never drove to. These are places a human geologist could walk to.
  • Same picture on two screens. The console and the wrist cuff run on one clock.

Factors we considered

  • Provenance. Every value carries Observed, Derived, Modeled, Assumed or Simulation. A value without a source is Assumed.
  • Checked against the real drive. We compared our slopes and route lengths with Perseverance's own track (1.6 % of it is steeper than our limit; our Tuff Cliff to Bright Angel leg is 581 m, the rover drove 582 m).
  • No invented data. We looked for a partner-agency dust value we could fetch without a login and found none, so the app shows no partner value.
  • Synthetic data stays labelled. The DEMO replay and test fixtures say SYNTHETIC on screen.
  • Credits. Every photo shows its credit line. No NASA logos, no mission patches, no AI-generated images.

Limitations

  • The cost model uses slope only, the same uphill and downhill; sand and rock fields are not in it. The speed curve comes from Earth hikers (Tobler 1993). The DTM has striping in the west of the area.
  • The slope limit, walking speed, EVA length and reserve come from lunar EVA requirements and a Mars suit design study (Assumed); no suited walk on Mars exists to check them against.
  • Conditions are shown beside the plan as go / no-go context; they do not change the route or the envelope yet. The storm alert is raised by the operator (Simulation), not by a forecast.
  • Radiation is one value measured by Curiosity at Gale crater, not at Jezero. MEDA has no dust opacity product. There is no geologic-map layer.
  • Some citations in the walk model have not yet been checked against the original documents (Tobler 1993 among them); the values they support are labelled Assumed.
  • The comparison with Perseverance's drives is a sanity check: a rover is not a human.

How we used AI

All six team members used Claude Code (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant. Before the event we used Claude to summarise the rules, survey public projects for this challenge, list the NASA data available and draft a work plan; it also proposed concept options, which the team discussed before choosing the science target, the site and the features. During the event we used it to plan each task, to find and quote sources, to write code, tests, data-processing scripts and notebooks, to debug, and to draft the docs, the stop cards, this page and the video script. The demo video is a screen recording of the running app; its edit, captions, title cards and background music (synthesised in code, no samples), and the layout of the images on this page, were made with Claude Code; the video and images carry a visible note saying so. The voice-over is a team member. The UI theme and our visual brief were drafted with it. A team member approved each plan and checked each result. We logged one line per task, and every AI-assisted commit names Claude as co-author. We used no AI-generated images.
